notes.24:3: Greek preserves the place name Eddaiem, where the Hebrew Masoretic Text reads "the rocks of the wild goats."
notes.24:4: Literally "to prepare himself," a Septuagint euphemism for relieving oneself (corresponding to the Hebrew idiom "to cover his feet").
notes.24:12: Greek reads "you are binding," whereas the Hebrew Masoretic Text reads "you are hunting" or "lying in wait for."
notes.24:20: Greek adds "in distress" and frames the verse as a conditional statement ("if anyone should find... then the Lord will repay him"), where the Hebrew Masoretic Text has a rhetorical question.
notes.24:23: Greek transliterates the place name Messara ("the narrow pass of Messara"), corresponding to the Hebrew term for "the stronghold."
notes.25:1: Greek reads "Armathaim" and "Maon," where the Hebrew Masoretic Text reads "Ramah" and "Paran."
notes.25:3: Greek reads "doglike," rendering the Hebrew tribal name "Calebite" etymologically from the root for "dog."
notes.25:22: Greek reads "to David," whereas the Hebrew Masoretic Text reads "to the enemies of David."
notes.25:28: In the Greek syntax the Lord is the subject fighting David's battle ("the Lord fights the battle of my lord"), whereas the Hebrew Masoretic Text says that David fights the battles of the Lord.
notes.25:43: Greek reads "from Israel," where the Hebrew Masoretic Text reads "of Jezreel."
notes.25:44: Greek reads the proper names "Ameis" and "Romma," where the Hebrew Masoretic Text reads "Laish" and "Gallim."
notes.26:1: The Greek reads 'Chelmath' (compare 'Hachilah' in 26:3 and the Hebrew text) and adds 'from the parched land,' also rendering Hebrew 'Gibeah' literally as 'the hill.'
notes.26:4: The Greek reads 'ready from Keilah' where the Hebrew Masoretic Text has 'for certain.'
notes.26:6: The Greek reads 'Abimelech' where the Hebrew text has 'Ahimelech.'
notes.26:10: The Greek uses a verb meaning 'discipline' where the Hebrew has 'strike,' and literally 'be added' (that is, gathered in death), reflecting a reading of Hebrew 'sapa' ('be swept away') as 'asap' ('gather/add').
notes.26:16: The Greek omits the negative particle, reading 'you who guard' where the Hebrew text has 'because you have not guarded.'
notes.26:20: The Greek reads 'to seek my life, just as the night raven pursues in the mountains' where the Hebrew has 'to seek a single flea, as one hunts a partridge in the mountains.'
notes.27:1: Throughout 1 Kingdoms, the Greek uses a common term meaning 'foreigners' where the Hebrew has 'Philistines.' Here 'I will be given over' translates a Greek verb literally meaning 'be added.'
notes.27:2: The Greek reads 'four hundred men' and 'Ammach' where the Hebrew text has 'six hundred men' and 'Maoch.'
notes.27:3: The Greek reads 'Ahinoam the Israelite' where the Hebrew text has 'Ahinoam the Jezreelitess,' and omits 'in Gath.'
notes.27:7: The Greek reads 'in the way of the foreigners' and 'four months' where the Hebrew text has 'in the country of the Philistines' and 'a year and four months.'
notes.27:8: This Greek clause is textually difficult and contains a doublet ('Gelampsour' and 'fortified places') corresponding to Hebrew 'from of old, as you go to Shur'; the Greek also omits the Girzites.
notes.27:10: The Greek reads 'Jesmega' and 'the Kenizzites' where the Hebrew text has 'the Jerahmeelites' and 'the Kenites.'
notes.27:11: The Greek text here shifts abruptly to the first-person singular ('I did not leave ... alive') where the Hebrew has third-person ('David would leave neither ... alive').
notes.28:3: The Greek uses the form 'Armathaim' (reflecting dual Ramathaim; compare 1 Samuel 1:1) where the Hebrew has 'Ramah.' 'Mediums' translates a Greek term literally meaning 'belly-speakers,' used for both necromancers and the familiar spirits speaking through them (compare 28:8).
notes.28:6: 'The manifestations' translates the Greek rendering of the Hebrew 'Urim' (compare Exodus 28:30).
notes.28:14: The Greek reads 'What did you recognize?' and 'an upright man' where the Hebrew text has 'What is his appearance?' and 'an old man.'
notes.28:16: The Greek reads 'has come to be with your neighbor' where the Hebrew text has 'has become your adversary.'
notes.28:19: The Greek reads 'tomorrow you and your sons with you will fall' where the Hebrew text has 'tomorrow you and your sons will be with me.'
notes.29:1: Greek allophyloi ("foreigners," literally "of another tribe") is the Septuagint's regular designation for the Philistines in 1 Samuel. The Greek also reads "Aeddon, which is in Israel," whereas the Hebrew Masoretic Text reads "the spring which is in Jezreel."
notes.29:3: The Greek reads "these passing through" where the Hebrew Masoretic Text reads "these Hebrews" (reflecting a different reading of the same Hebrew consonants), and specifies "this second year" rather than "these years."
notes.29:6: The Greek text lacks a negative particle at the end of the verse ("you are good"), whereas the Hebrew Masoretic Text reads "you are not good."
notes.29:10: The middle clauses ("and go to the place where I stationed you; and do not put a malicious word in your heart, for you are good before me") are a Septuagint plus absent from the Masoretic Text; in 29:11 the Greek similarly reads "guard the land of the foreigners" and "to fight against Israel" (MT: "return to the land of the Philistines" and "to Jezreel").
notes.30:1: The Greek reads "Keilah" for the town David entered before naming "Ziklag" twice later in the verse, whereas the Masoretic Text reads "Ziklag" throughout.
notes.30:8: The Greek transliterates the Hebrew word for a raiding band as geddour (also in 30:15, 23).
notes.30:9: The Greek numbers David's company at "four hundred men" rather than the Masoretic Text's "six hundred," and in 30:10 reads "the rest pursued with four hundred men" and "who sat across the brook Besor" (MT: "too exhausted to cross").
notes.30:14: The Greek reads "Cholthei" (MT: "Cherethites"), "Judea" (MT: "Judah"), and "Gilboa" (MT: "the Negev of Caleb").
notes.30:27: Across 30:27-30 the Septuagint preserves a longer, partly distinct list of towns (including Beth-zur, Geththor, Ammadei, Saphei, Estheie, Gath, Keimath, Saphek, Theimath, Carmel, the cities of Israel and Kenezei, Jerimuth, Beersheba, and Noo), and in 30:21 names the brook "Beana" rather than "Besor."
notes.31:2: The Greek names Saul's second son "Jonadab" (MT: "Abinadab") and uses singular "son of Saul."
notes.31:3: The Greek specifically states that Saul was wounded "in the abdomen" (hypochondria), whereas the Masoretic Text reads "badly wounded by the archers."
notes.31:9: The Greek reads "turned him over" (apostrephousin auton) where the Masoretic Text reads "cut off his head."
notes.31:10: The Greek names the city "Beth-em" here and "Beth-sam" in 31:12 (MT: "Beth-shan" in both), and in 31:12 specifies only the bodies of Saul and Jonathan rather than Saul and his sons.
notes.31:13: The Greek reads "under the field of Jabesh" (MT: "under the tamarisk tree in Jabesh"), and appends the opening notice of 2 Samuel 1:1 ("And it happened after Saul died... two days") directly to the end of the verse.

unplaced.text: And David arose and departed, and Jonathan went into the city.
